title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
oneLiner: The precise maths of an RL problem: states, actions, uncertain outcomes, rewards, and how to score the long-run value of a situation.

what.html:
A Markov decision process (MDP) writes the RL loop down exactly: a list of situations (states), the choices in each (actions), the chances of where each choice leads and what reward it gives, and a discount saying how much future rewards matter. Then we can ask how good each state is under a strategy (policy), and what the best strategy is.

Everyday versionA board game rulebook plus dice odds: from each square, each move has known chances of landing on other squares and scoring points. A good player thinks about where each move is likely to lead, not just the points right now.

why.html:
• Every RL algorithm is a way of solving (or approximating) the equations defined here.
  • It forces you to think clearly about what the state is and what reward you're giving.
  • Badly chosen rewards make agents do strange things.

how.title: The ingredients
how.html: States, actions, the probability p(s′, r | s, a) of landing in s′ with reward r, and a discount γ. Episodic problems also have terminal states.

how.title: The present is enough
how.html: The Markov property: the current state holds everything you need to predict what happens next; the path that got you here doesn't matter. In a noisy grid world, "move North" goes north 80% of the time and slips sideways 20%, so you have to think in probabilities.

how.title: Reward the goal, not the method
how.html: Any goal can be written as "maximise total reward". But reward what you want achieved (winning, a clean floor), not a method (capturing pieces, sucking up dirt), or the agent will game it.

how.title: Adding up the future
how.html: The return adds up future rewards, each multiplied by γ once more per step into the future. With γ = 0.5, rewards 1, 2, 3 are worth 2.75 now, but 3, 2, 1 are worth 4.25. Getting +1 forever with γ = 0.9 is worth 10.

how.title: How good is a state?
how.html: vπ(s) is the expected return from state s when following policy π. qπ(s, a) is the same but committing to action a first. They're linked: v is the policy's average of q.

how.title: Bellman: value = reward now + value next
how.html: A state's value equals the average, over your possible actions and where they lead, of the reward plus γ times the next state's value. Neighbours worth 2.3, 0.7, −0.4, 0.4 with γ = 0.9 and a random choice give 0.675.

how.title: The best possible values
how.html: The optimal value takes the best action instead of the average. Once you know the optimal values, the best policy is simply: in each state, pick the action that leads to the best expected reward plus next value.

demo.html: Press Play to spread values out from the +1 and −1 exits. Then change the cost of each step: a tiny cost makes the agent take the long safe path; a big cost makes it rush past the −1; a reward for living makes it avoid finishing at all.

example.html:
Same grid, different personality. With a step cost of −0.04 the best route from the bottom-left goes up the left side and along the top, well away from the −1 (values 0.81, 0.87, 0.92 along the top row). Raise the step cost to −2 and the agent heads for the nearest exit, even the −1, because every extra step hurts more than the −1 does.

Supplementary That's why adding a constant to every reward is safe in never-ending tasks but can change behaviour in tasks that end.

misunderstandings: Markov means the agent forgets everything.
The state must already contain what matters from the past.
Rewards should tell the agent how to do it.
Rewards define what to achieve; hints go elsewhere.
Discounting is only a maths trick.
It also encodes preferring sooner rewards and keeps sums finite.
v_π(s) is the policy-weighted average of q_π(s, a).
takeaways: MDP = states, actions, p(s′, r | s, a), rewards, γ.
Markov property: the current state is a sufficient summary.
Return Gₜ = Rₜ₊₁ + γGₜ₊₁; episodic vs continuing.
Bellman expectation: value = average of r + γ v(s′).
Bellman optimality uses max; greedy on v* or q* is optimal.
thirty: A finite MDP is defined by states, actions and dynamics p(s′, r | s, a) satisfying the Markov property, plus a discount γ. Rewards express goals (the reward hypothesis) and should reward what is to be achieved, not how. The return Gₜ = Σ γᵏRₜ₊ₖ₊₁ = Rₜ₊₁ + γGₜ₊₁ (e.g. [1,2,3] with γ = 0.5 → 2.75; +1 forever with γ = 0.9 → 10) applies to episodic and continuing tasks; adding a constant to rewards is harmless in continuing tasks but can change policies in episodic ones. Value functions v_π and q_π satisfy the Bellman expectation equation (a worked backup gives 0.675), and the optimal values v* and q* satisfy the Bellman optimality equations; acting greedily on them is optimal.
